challenges.title: A pattern is just code
challenges.instructions:
Welcome to the dojo. A Semgrep rule is a small YAML document with a handful of keys: an `id`, a
`message` that is shown with every finding, the `languages` it applies to, a `severity` label
(`INFO`, `WARNING` or `ERROR` — it does not change what matches) and, the part that does the work,
a `pattern`.

A pattern is not a regular expression. It is a piece of C# code, written exactly as you would type
it in a program, and Semgrep reports every place where that code occurs. The rule in the editor
looks for `Console.WriteLine("Press any key to exit.")` in a small test app from MQTTnet.

The prompt appears three times in the target: in two plain methods and once deep inside a `try`
block of an `async` method. One of the calls is even split over two lines. Semgrep compares syntax
trees, not text, so whitespace, line breaks and nesting depth never matter, and you never have to
describe the class or method around the code you are looking for.

Try running the rule as it is. Lines 21, 35 and 62 should light up, while `Console.Write(...)` on
line 55 and `Console.WriteLine(e)` on line 70 stay quiet: they are different code.
hints: There is nothing to fix in this first step: press Run and compare the highlighted lines with the `// ruleid:` comments in the target.
If you edited the pattern by accident, restore it to `Console.WriteLine("Press any key to exit.")`, including the final period inside the quotes.
challenges.followup_title: That is all a pattern is
challenges.followup:
Semgrep parsed your pattern with the same C# parser it used for the target, then searched the
target's syntax tree for an equal subtree. That is why it found the call inside `RunEmptyServer`
just as easily as the one nested in a `try` block of an `async` method, and why the call split
over lines 35-36 still matched: once the code is parsed, the line break is gone. You also did not
write the trailing semicolon. An expression pattern matches the expression wherever it appears,
whether it is a statement of its own or part of a bigger one.

The match is exact on the code, though. `Console.Write("...")` is a different method and
`Console.WriteLine(e)` has a different argument, so neither was reported.

**Try this:** change the literal to `"Press any key to exit"` (no period) and run again: every
match disappears, because that exact string never occurs in the file. Then try `Console.ReadLine()`
(four matches) and, since a pattern is just code, `using $X;` — it matches all six `using`
directives. The `$X` is a *metavariable*, a placeholder for "any name", and metavariables are the
topic of the next lessons.

challenges.title: The string wildcard "..."
challenges.instructions:
Semgrep patterns are written in the language you scan, so `Console.WriteLine("// GlobalSetup")` is a
complete pattern: a call to `Console.WriteLine` whose argument is exactly that string. Run the starter —
it reports a single call, on line 29, even though that line spells the string as
`"// " + "GlobalSetup"` (more on that once you have solved it).

This BenchmarkDotNet sample has five `Console.WriteLine` calls. We want to report every call that prints a
**hard-coded string**: lines 29, 34 and 39. The two calls on lines 19 and 24 print an interpolated string
whose value depends on a counter, so they must not match.

Try replacing the literal `"// GlobalSetup"` with `"..."` — three dots inside double quotes. It is the
wildcard for *any* string literal.
hints: The dots go *inside* the quotes: `"..."` means *any string literal*. A bare `...` between the parentheses would mean *any arguments* and would also match the two interpolated calls.
Only the argument changes; keep `Console.WriteLine(` and `)` exactly as in the starter.
The finished rule is `pattern: Console.WriteLine("...")`.
challenges.followup:
`"..."` stands for *any string literal*, so `Console.WriteLine("...")` matches every call whose argument
is a constant string, whatever its content.

Lines 29, 34 and 39 pass `"// " + "GlobalSetup"` and friends — not one literal in the source text, but
Semgrep runs **constant propagation** before matching and folds `"a" + "b"` into `"ab"`. That is why the
starter's exact string matched line 29, and why `"..."` matches all three concatenations. Lines 19 and 24
stay quiet: `$"// IterationSetup ({++setupCounter})"` is an interpolated string whose value is only known
at run time, and the same goes for a variable Semgrep cannot trace to a literal, such as a method
parameter in `Console.WriteLine(name)` — `"..."` accepts literals (folded ones included) and nothing else.

**Try this:** change the pattern to `Console.WriteLine($MSG)` — a metavariable matches *any* expression,
so all five calls light up. Then try `Console.WriteLine("// Benchmark")` and watch folding single out
line 39.

challenges.title: Ellipsis in argument lists
challenges.instructions:
Dapper's `Execute` takes the SQL text first and then whatever the caller needs: an optional
parameter object, followed by optional *named* arguments such as `commandType:` or `transaction:`.
In this test file the same method is called with one argument on some lines and with three on others.

We want to find every `Execute` call that passes a **parameter object** — lines 37 and 63, where
`args` is handed in right after the SQL string. The starter rule `$C.Execute("...", $P)` looks
right, but it matches nothing: arguments in a pattern are matched *by position*, so two arguments
in the pattern means exactly two arguments in the code, and both of our calls pass a third one.

Try adding `...` as a third argument, after `$P`. Inside an argument list the ellipsis stands for
*zero or more* further arguments, named ones included.
hints: Count the arguments on lines 37 and 63: after the SQL string and `args` there is a third, named argument `commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure`. The starter only has room for two.
`...` between the parentheses matches any number of arguments, including none. Put it where the extra argument appears — at the end.
The whole pattern is `$C.Execute("...", $P, ...)`.
challenges.followup:
`$C.Execute("...", $P, ...)` matches lines 37 and 63 because the argument list is read left to
right: `"..."` takes the SQL string, `$P` takes `args`, and the trailing `...` absorbs the named
`commandType:` argument. The one-argument calls on lines 21, 45 and 75 do not match — after the
string there is nothing left for `$P`, and a metavariable always has to bind *something*. Order
matters too: `$C.Execute($P, "...", ...)` finds nothing, because no call has a string literal in
second place.

Since `...` also matches *zero* arguments, a plain two-argument call such as
`connection.Execute("...", args)` would be reported as well.

**Try this:** change the pattern to `$C.Execute("...", ...)` — now all five calls match, because
`...` is satisfied by no extra arguments at all. Then try `$C.Execute($...ARGS)` and mention
`$...ARGS` in the `message`: an ellipsis *metavariable* binds the whole argument list, however
long it is.

challenges.title: Metavariables capture, string ellipsis restricts
challenges.instructions:
A **metavariable** is a placeholder that starts with `$` and matches exactly one expression:
`$TYPE` in `new Claim($TYPE, $VALUE)` matches whatever is passed as the first argument, and the
value it matched is available in the rule `message` as `$TYPE`.

The starter rule uses two metavariables, so it matches *every* `new Claim(...)` in this ASP.NET
Core sample. We only want the claim whose value is a **hard-coded string** (`"Member"`), not the one
that comes from a variable (`userName`).

Try replacing the second metavariable with `"..."` — the string wildcard matches any string
literal, and only string literals.
hints: `"..."` (three dots inside quotes) is a pattern for *any* string literal.
Keep `$TYPE` for the first argument; change only the second one.
challenges.followup:
`new Claim($TYPE, "...")` matches `new Claim("role", "Member")` because `"Member"` is a string
literal, while `userName` is a method parameter whose value Semgrep cannot know, so `"..."` does not
match it.

Notice that the match is reported on line 40 only: Semgrep reports the *expression* `new Claim(...)`, not the
whole initializer. Also notice that whitespace and line breaks in the target never matter.

**Try this:** change the pattern to `new Claim("...", $V)` — now both claims match, because both
first arguments are literals. Then try `new Claim($T, $T)` — nothing matches, because reusing a
metavariable requires *both* arguments to be the same expression.

challenges.title: Reusing a metavariable means equality
challenges.instructions:
In the previous step every metavariable had its own name. What happens when the **same**
metavariable appears twice in one pattern? Semgrep then requires both occurrences to bind to
the same expression: reusing a name means *equality*.

The target is a slice of `System.Double` from the .NET runtime. `IsNaN` uses a classic trick,
`return d != d;` — NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself. The starter pattern
`$A != $B` reports every inequality in the file: the bit test in `IsFinite` (line 21),
the `x != y` in `MaxNumber` (line 60) and the NaN trick in `IsNaN` (line 43).

We only want the self-comparison. Change the pattern so that both sides of `!=` use the
same metavariable — afterwards only `d != d` on line 43 should be reported.
hints: A metavariable name may appear more than once in a pattern. Two *different* names can bind two different expressions; one name can bind only one.
Keep the `!=` operator. Replace `$A` and `$B` with a single name, for example `$X`, on both sides.
The solution is `$X != $X`.
challenges.followup:
`$X != $X` matches `d != d` because the first `$X` binds to `d` and the second occurrence
has to be the *same* expression — which it is. In `(~bits & PositiveInfinityBits) != 0`
the first `$X` binds to `(~bits & PositiveInfinityBits)`, but the right side is `0`, so the
candidate is rejected; `x != y` fails for the same reason.

This is the general rule: within one pattern, a metavariable is bound on its first occurrence
and every further occurrence must be equal to that binding. It works for any expression, not
just simple identifiers.

Equality by reuse works for whole statements too: `if ($C) { $S; } else { $S; }` finds an `if`
whose branches are the same statement — a classic copy-paste bug — because `$S` must bind to
the same code twice. Nothing in this file has duplicated branches, so it matches nothing here.

**Try this:** change the operator to `==` — `$X == $X` — and run again. Now `value == value`
in `IsRealNumber` (line 82) is reported, while `bits == PositiveInfinityBits` in `IsInfinity`
(line 30) still is not. The grader will complain — line 43 is no longer matched and line 82
is not an expected line — but that is fine: you are exploring.

challenges.title: Statements, declarations and the ellipsis between them
challenges.instructions:
So far every pattern matched a single expression. A pattern can also be a **sequence of
statements**: write them one after another, each ending in `;`, and put `...` between them to
allow any number of other statements in between. Reusing `$C` in both statements ties them to
the *same* variable.

The starter looks for `$C = new SqlConnection(...); ... $C.Open();` — and finds nothing in this
repository class, although `GetBill` and `GetBillDescription` clearly create a connection and open
it a few lines later. The reason: `$C = ...;` is an **assignment** to an existing variable, but the
code contains **declarations** (`SqlConnection conn = ...;`), and Semgrep does not treat one as
the other.

Change the first statement of the pattern into a declaration so that both methods are reported.
The match must start at the `SqlConnection conn = ...` line (lines 20 and 41) and extend down to
the matching `conn.Open();` — this challenge grades the whole match range, not only the first line.
hints: Look at how `conn` is introduced in the code: it is *declared* together with its type, not assigned to a variable that already exists. Your pattern has to say the same.
A declaration in a pattern looks exactly like one in C#: `SqlConnection $C = new SqlConnection(...);`. (`var $C = ...` works as well — in a pattern, `var` accepts any declared type.)
Keep the rest unchanged, so the whole pattern reads `SqlConnection $C = new SqlConnection(...); ... $C.Open();`.
challenges.followup:
`SqlConnection $C = new SqlConnection(...);` is a *local declaration* statement, while
`$C = new SqlConnection(...);` is an *assignment* statement. They are different nodes in the syntax
tree, so the assignment pattern silently matched nothing — a common surprise when a pattern is
copied from a language without declarations. `var $C = ...` works too: in a pattern, `var` stands
for any declared type (the reverse is not true — `$T $C = ...` does not match a `var` declaration).

Each statement in the pattern ends with `;`, and the `...` between them stands for zero or more
statements. Because `$C` is reused, `Open()` must be called on the very variable that was
declared. The match Semgrep reports spans the whole sequence: from the declaration on line 20 down
to `conn.Open();` on line 30 (and 41 to 51 in the second method).

Two more things are worth knowing. The `...` also *descends* into nested blocks, so the pattern
would still match if `conn.Open()` sat inside a `try { }` or an `if` — but it never climbs *out*
of a block: a connection declared inside an `if` and opened after it is not a match. And a call
statement such as `$C.Open();` matches the call wherever it appears, even inside a bigger statement
like `SqlDataReader r = Helper(conn.Open());`.

**Try this:** append a third statement, `... $C.Close();`. Now nothing matches at all — neither
method ever closes its connection, which is exactly the resource leak the original project marks
with `CTSECISSUE: UnsafeDatabaseResourceRelease`. Then replace the whole pattern with the single
call statement `$X.$M();` and count the matches — five: besides the two `conn.Open();` lines it
reaches `sqlComm.ExecuteReader()` inside the `SqlDataReader DR = ...` declarations (lines 31 and
52) and `.FirstOrDefault()` at the end of the `return` on line 62, because call statements match
deeply. `Parameters.Add(...)` stays out: `$M()` with empty parentheses only matches calls without
arguments.

challenges.title: Patterns match at any depth — no wrapper needed
challenges.instructions:
Semgrep compares a pattern with **every** piece of code in the file, however deeply it is nested.
A pattern for a call such as `File.Delete(...)` is tried against each call inside each method,
`try` block, loop, local function and lambda. You never have to describe the code *around* the
call to reach it.

The starter rule tries to "get inside" a method first: `public void $M(...) { ... File.Delete(...); ... }`.
Run it and it reports nothing. In this Mouse Without Borders snippet the two deletes live in a
local function inside a `private static` method, and one of them is the body of a lambda
(`() => File.Delete(path)`). The wrapper did not help Semgrep look deeper; it only added
requirements (`public`, `void`, a block body) — and nothing in this snippet is `public`, so the
pattern never matches.

Change the pattern to the bare call `File.Delete(...)`. The rule must report exactly the two
deletes on lines 35 and 41 and stay quiet on the `File.Move` calls (lines 61 and 67).
hints: `public void $M(...) { ... }` is not a way *into* a method — it is an extra requirement on the method. Semgrep already searches inside every method, block and lambda on its own.
Keep only the part of the pattern that describes the call itself. The `...` between the parentheses stands for any arguments.
`pattern: File.Delete(...)` — one line, no braces.
challenges.followup:
`File.Delete(...)` is an *expression* pattern. Semgrep walks the whole syntax tree and compares
the pattern with every expression it meets, so it reaches line 35 (a statement inside `try` → `if`
inside a local function inside a private static method) and line 41 (the body of a lambda passed
as an argument) without being told the way there. The `File.Move` calls on lines 61 and 67 have the
same shape but a different name, so they stay quiet.

The wrapper failed for a subtler reason than it looks. `public void $M(...) { ... File.Delete(...); ... }`
*does* look into nested `try`, `if` and loop blocks — a statement `...` descends into inner blocks —
but it also demands a `public void` method with a block body, and it reports the **whole method**
as the match rather than the call. And a lambda without a block body, like line 41, can never be
found by a pattern that looks for `File.Delete(...);` as a statement.

Wrapping is the right tool only when the *context* is the point: "a `File.Delete` inside a `catch`
block", "only in methods marked `[HttpPost]`". Level 2 introduces `pattern-inside` for exactly that
job — it keeps the bare call as the reported match and adds the surrounding code as a separate
condition.

**Try this:** change the pattern to `$RET $M(...) { ... File.Delete(...); ... }`. Two matches
appear, but on lines 14 and 27 — the method and local-function headers — and the lambda on
line 41 is still missing.
Then try `File.$METHOD(...)`: now all four lines match and `$METHOD` is bound to `Delete` or `Move`.

challenges.title: The if ($C) pitfall
challenges.instructions:
Most patterns so far were *expressions* — a call, a `new`, a comparison. The statement-sequence
challenge showed the other kind: **statements**, each ending in `;`. An `if` is a statement too,
and statement patterns come with one rule that catches almost everybody once: the pattern has
to be a *complete* statement.

The target is OrchardCore's `EmailConfirmationController`. `SendVerificationEmail` guards the
`id` parameter twice with `string.IsNullOrEmpty` (lines 52 and 58). We want a rule that reports
exactly those two `if` statements — not the `== null` checks, not the compound condition on
line 65, and not the negated `!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(...)` on line 82.

The starter, `if (string.IsNullOrEmpty($X))`, looks like the obvious way to say "an `if` with
this condition". Run it: no error, but no match either. Semgrep could not read the pattern as a
statement (an `if` needs a body), so it read it as an expression instead — a *call to a method
named `if`* — and nothing in the file calls a method named `if`.

Change the starter into a complete `if` statement so that lines 52 and 58 are reported and
nothing else.
hints: Semgrep parses a pattern with the same grammar as the code. `if (x)` on its own is not a complete statement — but Semgrep's lenient pattern parser can read `if(x)` as an *expression*: a call to a method named `if`. That is what the starter looks for, so it finds nothing.
Give the `if` a body. Inside braces, `...` stands for any sequence of statements, so the body stays unconstrained.
`if (string.IsNullOrEmpty($X)) { ... }` is the canonical answer. `{ $S; ... }` (one statement, then anything) would also work, but it additionally demands a non-empty body.
challenges.followup:
`if (string.IsNullOrEmpty($X)) { ... }` is a complete statement, so Semgrep compares it with the
`if` statements in the file: the condition must be a call to `string.IsNullOrEmpty` with one
argument, and the body accepts any statement list — an assignment on line 52, a `return` on
line 58. It also matches an `if` without braces, because Semgrep compares statements, not
characters. The other checks have different conditions (`user == null`, `a && b`, the negated
`!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(...)`), so they are left alone.

Two details are worth remembering. The braces in the pattern do not require braces in the code:
`{ ... }` and one-statement bodies such as `{ $S; }` or `{ return NotFound(); }` also match a
brace-less body like `if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(id)) return NotFound();` (the two-element
workaround `{ $S; ... }` is the exception — it needs a real block), and an `else if` chain is
just an `if` nested in an `else`, so a chain yields one match per `if`. And names are compared
textually: this code says `string`, so `String.IsNullOrEmpty($X)` would find nothing here,
although both spellings mean the same type in C#.

If you have the CLI at hand, `semgrep show dump-pattern csharp 'if ($C)'` shows the pitfall
directly: the dump is an expression (`E(Call(...))`) whose callee is the identifier `if`.

**Try this:** replace the body with `{ return NotFound(); }` — now only line 58 matches, because
the braces describe the body, not just the header. Then use the general form `if ($C) { ... }`:
it reports all eight `if` statements in the file, which is the usual starting point when you
later narrow the condition down with `pattern-not` or `metavariable-pattern`.

challenges.title: Method definitions and modifiers
challenges.instructions:
A method definition is a pattern too. `$RET $M(...) { ... }` reads as: any return type, any
method name, any parameter list, any body — so it matches **every** method in this ASP.NET Core
Identity sample controller, including the private helpers at the bottom.

Modifiers work as a *required subset*: whatever modifiers you write in the pattern must be present on
the method, and any modifiers you leave out are allowed to be there or not. `static` in a pattern
excludes instance methods; leaving `static` out matches both.

We want only the controller's HTTP endpoints — the `public` methods (four of them, one of which is
`async`). Change the pattern so that the three `private` helpers no longer match.

Note where the ▶ markers sit: a method's match *starts at its first attribute* (`[HttpGet]`), because
attributes are part of the declaration — the shaded lines below each marker are the rest of the match.
hints: Put a modifier in front of `$RET`.
`public $RET $M(...) { ... }` — `async` and the attributes do not need to be mentioned; they are simply allowed.
challenges.followup:
`public $RET $M(...) { ... }` requires `public` and nothing else: `async` is an extra modifier the

challenges.title: Attributes on methods
challenges.instructions:
ASP.NET Core routes requests to controller methods by their **attributes**: `[HttpGet]`,
`[HttpPost]`, `[HttpPost("import")]` and so on. In Semgrep, attributes are written in front of the
definition pattern, exactly as in C#.

The starter pattern `[$A] $R $M(...) { ... }` puts a metavariable in the attribute position. Run it
and look closely: it matches `[HttpGet]` and `[HttpPost]`, but not `[HttpGet("export")]` — an
attribute *with arguments* is a different shape, just like `Foo` and `Foo(1)` are different.

We want the two POST endpoints, `Post` and `Import`, and nothing else. Write the attribute with
an argument-list wildcard so that both `[HttpPost]` and `[HttpPost("import")]` are accepted.
hints: Name the attribute and give it `(...)` as argument list.
`[HttpPost(...)] $R $M(...) { ... }` — `(...)` also matches an attribute written without any parentheses.
challenges.followup:
`[HttpPost(...)]` matches both spellings: Semgrep treats an attribute without parentheses as one
with an empty argument list, and `...` accepts zero arguments. `[HttpPost]` on its own would only
match the bare form.

Attributes are matched as a *subset*: a method decorated with `[Authorize] [HttpPost]` still
matches a pattern that mentions only `[HttpPost(...)]`. Order does not matter either.

**Try this:** `[HttpGet(...)] $R $M(...) { ... }` finds the three GET endpoints. Then try
`[Route(...)] class $C : Controller { ... }` — attributes on classes work the same way, and this
is a handy `pattern-inside` for "only inside controllers" in Level 2.

challenges.title: Named arguments match in any order
challenges.instructions:
C# lets a caller pass an argument **by name**. Dapper's query methods all take an optional
`commandType`, and this test file always passes it as `commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure` —
as the second argument on line 82, as the third on line 61, and on line 39 *every* argument is
named, `sql:` and `param:` included.

The starter rule `$CONN.$METHOD(..., CommandType.StoredProcedure)` treats `CommandType.StoredProcedure`
as an ordinary positional argument, and it matches nothing: the name is part of a named argument, so a
positional argument in a pattern never matches a named argument in the code.

Change the last argument of the pattern into a named argument, `commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure`,
and put `...` on both sides of it. The rule should then report the three calls on lines 39, 61 and 82
and leave lines 24 and 26 alone.

One thing to watch: the pattern now contains `commandType:` followed by a space, which YAML would read
as a nested key. Keep the pattern inside the quotes the starter already uses.
hints: A named argument in a pattern is written the way C# writes it: `name: value`. The name must be the parameter's name, here `commandType`.
Semgrep matches a named argument by its name, not by its position, so surround it with `...` on both sides and it is found wherever the caller put it.

If the rule fails to parse as YAML (`bad indentation of a mapping entry` in the browser, `mapping values are not allowed here` in the CLI), the `commandType:` inside the pattern is being parsed as a key — the whole pattern must stay in quotes.
The whole pattern is `'$CONN.$METHOD(..., commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure, ...)'`, quotes included.
challenges.followup:
`$CONN.$METHOD(..., commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure, ...)` matches lines 39, 61 and 82
because Semgrep matches a named argument **by its name**, not by its place in the list; the two `...`
absorb whatever else the caller wrote before and after it. One pattern therefore covers a call where
`commandType:` is the second argument, one where it is the third, and one where all three arguments
are named. Line 24 is not reported: `direction:` and `size:` are different names.

The starter failed because `CommandType.StoredProcedure` without a name is a *positional* argument,
and positional and named arguments never match each other — in either direction.

The trailing `...` matters as soon as something follows the named argument: on line 24 `size: 255`
comes after `direction: ParameterDirection.Output`, so `$P.Add(..., direction: ParameterDirection.Output)`
misses that line while `$P.Add(..., direction: ParameterDirection.Output, ...)` finds it.

**Try this:** replace the first `...` with `$SQL`. Lines 61 and 82 still match, but line 39 drops
out — there the SQL text is passed as `sql: "..."`, and a positional metavariable does not bind a
named argument either. Then try `$P.Add(..., direction: ParameterDirection.Output, dbType: DbType.Int32, ...)`:
it matches line 22 although the code lists `dbType:` first, because the order of named arguments
in the pattern does not matter.

challenges.title: Typed metavariables
challenges.instructions:
Umbraco's `HashGenerator` feeds values of many types into one `StreamWriter`. Every `Add…` method
ends up calling `_writer.Write(...)`, so the starter pattern matches six calls. Suppose we only care
about the call that writes a **string**.

A **typed metavariable** `(string $X)` matches an expression only when Semgrep can tell that its
type is `string`. Semgrep learns types from declarations it can see in the same file: parameters,
fields, properties, locals and literals. It does *not* infer the return type of a method call such
as `s.ToUpperInvariant()` — not even when the method is declared in the same file.

Change the argument of the pattern to a typed metavariable so that only `_writer.Write(s)` inside
`AddString` matches.
hints: The syntax is a parenthesised type and metavariable: `(string $X)`.
`_writer.Write((string $X))` — two sets of parentheses: the call's and the typed metavariable's.
challenges.followup:
`s` is declared as `string s` in the parameter list of `AddString`, so `(string $X)` accepts it. In
`AddCaseInsensitiveString`, the argument is `s.ToUpperInvariant()` — a method call, and Semgrep does
not infer the return types of calls, so it is *not* matched even though a human knows it is a
string. The `i` parameters of `AddInt` and `AddLong` are an `int` and a `long`, `o` is an `object`
and `d.Ticks` is a member of a `DateTime` — none of them is a `string`, so they are rejected.

This is the rule of thumb for typed metavariables: they are precise but conservative. Unknown types
never match, so use them to *narrow* a pattern, never to *find* everything of a type.

**Try this:** change the type to `(long $X)` — `AddLong` matches, and so does `AddInt`, because
Semgrep treats `int` and `long` as compatible integer types; `d.Ticks` does not match although it
is a `long` too, because Semgrep does not resolve members of `DateTime`. Then try `(object $X)` —
only `AddObject` matches: `object` is not treated as "anything".

challenges.title: The deep expression operator <... e ...>
challenges.instructions:
This intentionally vulnerable MVC controller (IssueBlot.NET) takes a request parameter `input`
and glues it into four SQL strings before handing them to an Entity Framework context — and into
a fifth one for a SharePoint `FullTextSqlQuery`.

The starter rule `$CTX.$M(input)` says: *some method on some object is called with `input` as the
argument*. That matches nothing here, because the argument is never `input` itself — it is
`"select * from students " + input`, a bigger expression that merely **contains** `input`.

The **deep expression operator** `<... e ...>` means "an expression that contains `e` anywhere
inside it". Change the argument of the starter pattern so that all four query calls match, and
nothing else does. One of the four calls has *three* arguments — remember what `...` does in an
argument list.
hints: Wrap `input` in the deep expression operator: `<... input ...>`.
`$CTX.$M(<... input ...>)` matches three of the four calls — the fourth has two more arguments after the SQL string.
Surround the deep expression with argument ellipses: `$CTX.$M(..., <... input ...>, ...)`.
challenges.followup:
`<... input ...>` matches any expression with `input` somewhere inside — `"..." + input` here, but it
would equally match `Sanitize(input)`, `input.Trim()` or `a + (b + input)`. That is exactly what you
want when you are hunting for user input that *flows into* an API, whatever is done to it on the way.
The `...` on either side of the deep expression let the tainted argument sit at any position in a
call of any arity — without them, `$M(<... input ...>)` only matched the three single-argument calls.

The generic calls `CreateQuery<Student>(...)` and `ExecuteStoreQuery<Student>(...)` still match
`$M(...)`: type arguments do not get in the way of a method-name metavariable.

The `QueryText = "..." + input` line in the object initializer is not reported — it is an
assignment, not a call, so `$CTX.$M(...)` cannot match it.

**Try this:** replace the pattern with `$CTX.$M(..., <... "..." + input ...>, ...)` — still four matches.
Then try `<... input ...>` on its own as the whole pattern: Semgrep reports *every* expression that
contains `input` — the whole call, the `"..." + input` concatenation inside it and the bare `input`
itself — so you get 19 overlapping matches, now including the `QueryText` line.

challenges.title: Ellipsis in method chains
challenges.instructions:
Fluent APIs build objects with long dotted chains. Serilog's own tests configure loggers as
`new LoggerConfiguration().<anything>.CreateLogger()`, and the "anything" differs every time:
one sink, two sinks, a wrapper with a lambda, a minimum-level switch.

The starter pattern spells out one exact chain, so it only finds the two configurations whose
middle is nothing but a single `.WriteTo.Sink(...)` step. Three of the five chains are missed:
the one with an extra `.MinimumLevel` step, the one with two sinks, and the wrapper.

Semgrep has an ellipsis for chains: writing `. ... .` between two members means "any number of
property accesses or method calls in between". Change the pattern so that every
`new LoggerConfiguration()` … `.CreateLogger()` chain matches, whatever happens in the middle.
hints: Keep the two ends, `new LoggerConfiguration()` and `.CreateLogger()`, and replace everything between them with the chain ellipsis.

Mind the dots — a dot, a space, three dots, a space, a dot: `new LoggerConfiguration(). ... .CreateLogger()`. Without the spaces, `()....CreateLogger()` parses as a range expression and silently matches nothing.
challenges.followup:
`. ... .` skips both property accesses (`.WriteTo`, `.MinimumLevel`) and calls
(`.Sink(...)`, `.ControlledBy(...)`, `.DummyWrapper(...)`), so all five chains match — including the
one-liner, because line breaks never matter, and the one whose middle step takes a lambda.

The match starts at `new LoggerConfiguration()` and ends after `.CreateLogger()`; Semgrep reports
the whole expression, not just the first line.

**Try this:** `new LoggerConfiguration(). ... .WriteTo.Sink($S). ... .CreateLogger()` — the
wrapper-based configuration drops out (its sink is passed inside a lambda, not as a direct chain
step). Then `$C. ... .CreateLogger()` — the receiver becomes anything, which would also match a
chain that starts from an existing configuration variable. Here all five still match, but each
several times: every way of splitting a chain between `$C` and the ellipsis is its own match.

challenges.title: pattern-either — any of these
challenges.instructions:
PowerToys Run's value generator keeps a table of hash algorithms — from MD5 to SHA-512. The
developers even left `#pragma` notes on the two that .NET's analyzers flag as broken (MD5) or
weak (SHA-1).

A single `pattern:` can express one shape. To say "this **or** that", a rule uses
`pattern-either:` with a list of alternatives; a match on any of them counts.

The starter finds `MD5.Create()`. Change it into a `pattern-either` that also reports
`SHA1.Create()`, while the SHA-2 family stays untouched.
hints: Replace `pattern:` with `pattern-either:` followed by a YAML list of `- pattern:` entries.
Two alternatives: `MD5.Create()` and `SHA1.Create()`.
challenges.followup:
`pattern-either` is an OR over complete patterns. Each alternative is matched on its own and the
results are merged, so a line that two alternatives both hit still counts once here — grading is
by line. (The CLI also drops duplicate findings on the same range; the older browser engine keeps
them apart in the "raw matches" list.)

It can be nested anywhere a pattern is allowed — inside `patterns:` (AND) to express
"one of these, AND not inside that", or inside a taint source/sink list. A production rule for weak
hashing would add more alternatives for the older constructors, such as
`new MD5CryptoServiceProvider()` and `new SHA1Managed()`.

**Try this:** add `- pattern: $ALG.Create()` as a third alternative — all five table entries match,
because the alternatives are independent and the last one is the loosest. Then swap `pattern-either`
for `patterns`: now the entries are ANDed, and nothing can be both `MD5.Create()` and `SHA1.Create()`,
so you get zero matches.

challenges.title: pattern-not — subtract what you don't want
challenges.instructions:
Level 2 is about **composing** patterns. A `patterns:` block is a logical AND: every entry must
hold for a match to survive. The simplest entry after `pattern` is `pattern-not`, which *removes*
matches.

This ASP.NET Core sample controller redirects three times. Two redirects go to the fixed URL `"/"`
and are harmless; the third sends the user to `returnUrl`, a value that came from the request and
needs a local-URL check. (This sample does check, on line 43 — subtracting *guarded* redirects is a
later challenge; here every redirect to a variable should be reported.) The starter matches all three.

Add a `pattern-not` entry so that redirects to a string literal are excluded and only
`Redirect(returnUrl)` remains.
hints: Under `patterns:` add a second list item: `- pattern-not: ...`.
The thing to exclude is a redirect to *any* string literal: `Redirect("...")`.
challenges.followup:
`pattern-not: Redirect("...")` removes every match whose range is *also* matched by that pattern.
The two `Redirect("/")` calls are literal redirects and disappear; `Redirect(returnUrl)` stays.

Order inside `patterns:` does not matter — Semgrep evaluates positive patterns first, then the
negative ones. And a `patterns:` block with a single `pattern` entry is the same as a bare
`pattern:`; the block only becomes interesting once you add filters.

**Try this:** flip it around — keep `pattern: Redirect($U)` and add `pattern-not: Redirect($V)`
with a *different* metavariable name. Everything disappears: `$V` is not bound by the positive
pattern, so it is free to match any argument and the negative pattern cancels every match.
(`pattern-not: Redirect($U)` cancels everything too — at the same range the same name binds the
same argument.) Metavariables *do* carry across the entries of a `patterns:` block; the next
challenges are built on exactly that.

challenges.title: pattern-inside restricts — and binds
challenges.instructions:
You learned in Level 1 that a bare `Redirect(...)` already matches inside every method, so
`pattern-inside` is never needed just to "get inside". Its job is to **restrict**: keep only
matches that lie within some enclosing code. The starter's `pattern-inside: $R $M(...) { ... }`
restricts nothing — every call is inside some method — so all four redirects match.

The trick that makes `pattern-inside` powerful is **metavariable unification**: a metavariable bound
in the enclosing pattern must take the *same value* in the inner pattern. Here both files
redirect to a *string parameter of the method itself* (`returnUrl`), while the harmless redirects go
to the literal `"/"`.

Change the two patterns so that the redirect argument and a `string` parameter of the enclosing
method share one metavariable name. The literal redirects must drop out.
hints: Give the parameter a name in the method pattern: `$R $M(..., string $P, ...) { ... }`.
Use the *same* name in the call: `Redirect($P)`. A literal `"/"` can never equal a parameter name.
challenges.followup:
`pattern-inside: $R $M(..., string $P, ...) { ... }` binds `$P` to each string parameter of a method
(`userName`, `password`, `returnUrl`), and `pattern: Redirect($P)` only matches when the argument
*is* one of those names. `Redirect("/")` cannot unify with any parameter and is gone.

Compare with a shallow version: `patterns` with `pattern: Redirect($U)` and
`pattern-inside: $R $M(..., string $P, ...) { ... }` still keeps `Login`'s `Redirect("/")`, because `$U`
and `$P` are unrelated names. (Only `Logout`'s `Redirect("/")` drops out — and only because `Logout()`
has no `string` parameter at all, not because of what it redirects to.) Unification only happens
through *shared* metavariable names.

**Try this:** add `[HttpGet]` in front of the inside pattern — only AspGoat's `OpenRedirect` remains,
since the aspnetcore action is `[HttpPost]`. Then remove it again and add
`class AccountController : Controller { ... }` as a second `pattern-inside` — now only `Login` remains:
two `pattern-inside` entries are ANDed, like everything under `patterns:`.

challenges.title: pattern-not-inside — unless it is guarded
challenges.instructions:
Two redirects to a request-controlled `returnUrl`. The aspnetcore sample is safe: its redirect sits
inside `if (Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)) { ... }`. AspGoat's `OpenRedirect` only checks for `null` — a
textbook open redirect.

The starter already excludes literal redirects, so it reports both parameter redirects. We want the
guarded one gone. `pattern-not-inside` is the negative twin of `pattern-inside`: it drops matches
that lie within the given code, and — like `pattern-inside` — it unifies metavariables with the main
pattern.

Add a `pattern-not-inside` entry for an `if` whose condition is `Url.IsLocalUrl(...)` applied to
the *same* value that is being redirected to.
hints: The enclosing code is an `if` statement; write it as a complete statement with a body.
Reuse `$U`: `if (Url.IsLocalUrl($U)) { ... }` — the guard must test the redirected value, not just any value.
challenges.followup:
`pattern-not-inside: if (Url.IsLocalUrl($U)) { $S; ... }` removes the aspnetcore match because that
`Redirect(returnUrl)` is nested in an `if` guarding exactly `returnUrl`. AspGoat's `if (returnUrl != null)`
is an `if` too, but its condition is not `Url.IsLocalUrl(...)`, so the redirect stays reported.

Unification matters here: with `if (Url.IsLocalUrl($OTHER))` the exclusion would also fire for a
redirect to `b` guarded by a check of `a` — a classic false negative.

**Try this:** change the guard to `if (Url.IsLocalUrl($U)) { ... } else { ... }` — the aspnetcore
redirect has an `else` branch, so it is still excluded; AspGoat's is not. Then remove the
`pattern-not` entry and watch `Redirect("/")` come back: every entry under `patterns:` is independent.

challenges.title: The ellipsis never climbs out of a block
challenges.instructions:
A statement-sequence pattern `A; ... B;` matches when `B` comes *after* `A`. The ellipsis may dive
into nested blocks that follow `A` — a `try`, an `if`, a loop — and it may come back up again. What
it can never do is climb **above the block in which the sequence started**.

The starter starts *inside* the `try` block of `InsecureDeserialization` (`new StringReader(xml)`),
continues to the `Deserialize` call in the same block, and then asks for `return View();` — which
lives in the method body, one level above the `try`. Run it: **no match**.

Remove the part of the pattern that would require climbing out of the `try`, so that the flow
from the `StringReader` to `Deserialize` is reported.
hints: Which statement in the pattern is outside the `try` block in the code, while the sequence started inside it?
Delete the trailing `...` and `return View();` — the pattern then stays inside the `try`.
challenges.followup:
Think of `...` between statements as "keep walking forward": it may go down into nested blocks
and back out to the level it started from, but never higher. Starting at `new StringReader(xml)`
inside the `try`, the walk can reach `Deserialize(...)` in the same block, but `return View();`
is outside that block — unreachable.

Had the sequence started at `var xml = RequestUtils.GetIfDefined(Request, "xml");` in the method
body, the very same trailing `... return View();` would have been fine: from there the walk goes

challenges.title: metavariable-regex — a regex on what a metavariable captured
challenges.instructions:
This model class from a deliberately vulnerable API (dvcsharp-api) declares four string
constants. Three are harmless role names; the fourth is a 64-character hex string used to sign JWTs
— a hard-coded secret.

`public const string $N = $V;` captures every constant. To keep only the secret we need to look
*at the text* that `$V` captured. That is what `metavariable-regex` does: inside a `patterns:`
block it filters matches by running a regular expression over the source text bound to a
metavariable.

Add a `metavariable-regex` entry that keeps only values consisting of 32 or more hex digits.
Remember that `$V` captured the literal *including its quotes*.
hints: The entry is `- metavariable-regex:` with two indented keys, `metavariable: $V` and `regex: ...`, and sits under `patterns:` next to the `- pattern:` line. Use that block form — a one-line `{metavariable: $V, regex: ...}` mapping breaks on the `[` and `{` inside the regex.
Anchor the regex and include the quotes: `^"[0-9a-f]{32,}"$`.
challenges.followup:
`metavariable-regex` sees the raw source text of the binding — for a string literal that is
`"f449a71c…"`, quotes included, which is why the regex starts with `"`. It is also *left-anchored*:
Semgrep only tries the regex at the beginning of the captured text, so the bare `[0-9a-f]{32,}`
finds nothing here (the text starts with a quote). The end is not anchored — `"[0-9a-f]{32}` would
match too — so the closing `"$` is what stops a long hex prefix inside a longer literal from
passing. The leading `^` is redundant but harmless; for a "contains" test, start the regex with `.*`.

**Try this:** run `metavariable-regex` on `$N` instead, with `regex: (?i)secret|token|password` — a
common way to flag suspicious *names* rather than values. `TokenSecret` is still reported, but only
because it *starts* with `Token`: change the regex to `(?i)secret` and the finding disappears;
`(?i).*secret` brings it back. Then keep both the name check and the value check as two entries
under `patterns:` and see that they are ANDed.

challenges.instructions:
The `Import` action deserializes the raw request body with an `XmlSerializer`. The starter rule
finds the call, and this time the *line* is not the problem — the **range** is.

Look at the result after running the starter: the reported range is the whole call
`serializer.Deserialize(reader)` — line 50, columns 37 to 67. Security findings are more
useful when they point at the untrusted *input*, and taint rules (coming up in Level 3) need to
know which sub-expression carries the data.

`focus-metavariable: $X` inside a `patterns:` block narrows the reported range to whatever `$X`
captured, without changing which places match. Add it to the starter so the finding covers only
`reader` (line 50, columns 60 to 66).

This challenge is graded on exact ranges (start and end column), not just lines.
hints: The starter binds two metavariables: `$S` (the serializer) and `$R` (the argument). Which one captures `reader`? That is the one to focus on.
Add `- focus-metavariable: $R` as a second entry under `patterns:`.
challenges.followup:
Same line, smaller range: `focus-metavariable` re-anchors the finding on the binding of `$R`. Two
consequences worth knowing:

* Everything else in the rule still applies — `pattern-not`, `pattern-inside` and friends filter
  the *original* match; focusing happens last. (Add `- pattern-not: reader` to your solution: the
  finding survives, because the exclusion is checked against the full call, not against `reader`.)
* In taint rules, each `pattern-sources` / `pattern-sinks` entry accepts the same `patterns:`
  blocks, and `focus-metavariable` is how you say "the source is this parameter" or "only this
  argument of the sink is dangerous".

wrapper, write `pattern: $S.Deserialize($R)` on its own and put `focus-metavariable: $R` next to
it at the top level of the rule: the match is back to the full call. `focus-metavariable` is only
honoured inside a `patterns:` list — at the top level the browser warns about an unknown key, and
the `semgrep` CLI ignores it without a word (even `--validate` is happy).

challenges.title: pattern-regex sees raw text — even comments
challenges.instructions:
Every pattern so far worked on the *syntax tree*, which is why comments, whitespace and line
breaks never mattered. `pattern-regex` is different: it runs a regular expression over the raw
text of the file. That makes it the only way to match things the parser throws away — such as
the `// CTSECISSUE:` markers the IssueBlot authors left above each intentional bug.

The starter matches every marker, six in all. We only want the five SQL-injection markers; the
`MVCViewCodeInjection` one at the bottom must not match.

Inside a `patterns:` block, `pattern-not-regex` removes every match that contains a match of its
own regex (or sits inside one). Write a `pattern-not-regex` entry that drops the code-injection
marker.
hints: Add a second entry under `patterns:`: `- pattern-not-regex: '...'`.
`pattern-not-regex: 'CodeInjection'` — the regex only needs to match somewhere inside the marker it should remove.
challenges.followup:
`pattern-regex` reported the six comment lines because regular expressions see the source as
text; `pattern-not-regex: 'CodeInjection'` then removed the one match that contains a
`CodeInjection` match. A match is dropped when it contains, or sits inside, a `pattern-not-regex`
match — a partial overlap is not enough (the docs say "any overlap", but the engine checks
containment). The regex flavour is PCRE2 in multiline mode, so `^` and `$` also match at line
boundaries, and character classes and groups work as usual — but a regex knows nothing about C#:
it matches just as happily inside a string literal or a comment as in code.

Regex operators combine with syntax patterns: a common idiom is `pattern: Foo("...")` plus
`pattern-regex: 'password'` under `patterns:` to require a substring in the matched text (the
finding is then reported at the regex hit, the inner of the two ranges). And since regexes see
*everything*, a sloppy one would even match this site's own `// ruleid:` annotations — which is
why the marker regex is anchored on `CTSECISSUE`.

**Try this:** replace the solution with a single `pattern-regex: 'CTSECISSUE:\s*SQL\w*'` — same
five matches, no `pattern-not-regex` needed. Then compare `pattern-regex: 'input'` with the
syntax pattern `pattern: input`: the text search reports one hit more. Find it and work out why
the syntax pattern skips it.

challenges.title: options — constant propagation on and off
challenges.instructions:
This JWT is created with `issuer: issuer` — a local variable, not a literal. Yet the local was
assigned the literal `"http://localhost.local/"` earlier in the same method (line 27). Whether the pattern
`new $T(..., issuer: "...", ...)` (a named argument with a string-literal value) matches depends on
**constant propagation**.

By default Semgrep tracks constants: a local assigned a literal, a `const` field, or a
concatenation of literals is treated as if the literal were written in place. The starter turns
that off with `options: {constant_propagation: false}` and therefore finds nothing.

Rule-level `options:` toggle engine behaviours for one rule. Change the option so that the token
construction is reported.
hints: Look at the `options:` block; the value of `constant_propagation` is the only thing to change. (The pattern stays quoted: it contains `issuer:` which unquoted YAML would take for a mapping key and reject.)
`constant_propagation: true` (or simply delete the `options:` block — true is the default).
challenges.followup:
With propagation on, Semgrep follows `issuer` back to `"http://localhost.local/"` and lets `"..."`
match, exactly as if the literal were inline. The named-argument syntax `issuer: "..."` matches the
argument by *name*, so its position among the other arguments does not matter.

Constant propagation reaches further than locals: Semgrep also folds `const` fields —
`Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(secret)` with `secret = TokenSecret` matches `$ENC.GetBytes("...")` as
well. This challenge sticks to the `issuer` local so that the switch has one visible effect.

`options:` holds a handful of such switches. Two others: `symmetric_eq` (treat `a == b` and
`b == a` alike) and `taint_unify_mvars` (require the same metavariable binding at a taint source
and sink), which you will meet in Level 3.

**Try this:** set `constant_propagation: false` again and change the pattern to
`new $T(..., issuer: issuer, ...)` — an exact name works regardless of propagation, but it is
fragile. Then try `new $T(..., audience: "...", ...)` with propagation on.

challenges.title: paths — which files a rule looks at
challenges.instructions:
Not every finding is worth reporting everywhere. This Dapper file lives at
`tests/Dapper.Tests/ProcedureTests.cs`, and stored-procedure calls in a *test suite* are exactly
what you would expect. The starter rule reports all three of them.

A rule can restrict the files it applies to with a top-level `paths:` key holding `include:` and
`exclude:` lists of glob patterns, matched against each file's path relative to the project root
(the Git root, or the scanned directory when there is no repository).

Add a `paths:` block that excludes everything under `tests/`, so that this file produces **zero**
findings. (The site knows the target's path; every call is marked `○ must not match`.)
hints: The block is top-level, next to `pattern:` — `paths:` containing `exclude:` with a list of globs.
`exclude: ["tests/**"]` — the `**` glob matches any number of directory levels.
challenges.followup:
`paths.exclude: ["tests/**"]` removes the file from the rule's scope before any pattern is tried,
so nothing is reported. `include:` works the other way round (only listed globs are scanned), and
both accept several entries.

Path filtering is applied per rule, which is why it is a rule key and not a CLI flag; the CLI flags
`--include` / `--exclude` do the same for a whole run. Semgrep even agrees with you about test
code: when you point the CLI at a directory, its built-in `.semgrepignore` defaults already skip
`test/` and `tests/`; a file named explicitly on the command line (which is how `scripts/check.py`
runs this target) is scanned regardless. The browser engine on this site applies `paths` to the
target's path (`tests/Dapper.Tests/ProcedureTests.cs`) in the same way, so the exclude takes effect
here too.

**Try this:** change it to `include: ["src/**"]` — same effect for this file. Then try
`exclude: ["*Tests.cs"]`: a glob without a slash matches the file *name* anywhere in the tree.

challenges.title: pattern-regex inside a syntax match — look into a string literal
challenges.instructions:
RestSharp keeps a dozen regular expressions in `static readonly Regex` fields. One of them,
`NewDateRegex`, was [CVE-2021-27293](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9pq7-rcxv-47vq): the
group `(-?\d+)*` repeats a group that can itself repeat, so a hostile server response makes the
matcher backtrack for a very long time (ReDoS). We want to find regex literals that quantify a
whole group with `*` or `+` — the text `)*` or `)+`.

A syntax pattern cannot help here: `"..."` matches a *whole* string literal and has no way to
look at the characters inside it. `pattern-regex` can, because it works on the source text.
The starter's `pattern: new Regex("...")` matches all twelve fields; combine it with a
`pattern-regex` so that only the constructor call whose literal contains `)*` or `)+` remains.

Write the `pattern-regex` entry. Remember that `)` is a regex metacharacter, so it needs a
backslash — and put the regex in single quotes so YAML leaves the backslash alone.
hints: Add a second entry under `patterns:`, `- pattern-regex: '...'`. Under `patterns:` the regex hit must lie inside the range of the syntax match, so the regex is effectively searched *within* each `new Regex("...")` call.
`pattern-regex: '\)[*+]'` — an escaped closing parenthesis followed by a star or a plus.
challenges.followup:
Under `patterns:`, a `pattern-regex` entry is ANDed with the syntax pattern by *range*: the regex
hit has to fall inside a range that `pattern: new Regex("...")` matched, so the eleven other
fields drop out even though they are perfectly good `new Regex(...)` calls. The finding is
reported at the regex hit — the inner of the two ranges. Note that `"..."` happily matched the
verbatim literal `@"newDate\((-?\d+)*\)"`: the `@` prefix is part of the literal token, and the
regex saw the raw text with its backslashes exactly as written in the file.

This is a rough heuristic — `([A-Z]+)` is harmless because the `+` is *inside* the group — but it
found the real CVE. The exact tool for the job is `metavariable-analysis` with `analyzer: redos`,
which parses the captured regex and reports only patterns with exponential worst-case behaviour.

**Try this:** swap the regex for `'\{\d+\}'` to find bounded repetitions such as `{4}` (one
field), then for `'\)\?'` (which field has an optional group?). Finally delete the
`pattern:` line and run the regex on its own: same result in this file — until someone adds a
comment that mentions `)*`.

challenges.title: pattern-regex named groups — capture text into a metavariable
challenges.instructions:
ExcelDataReader has to speak the legacy Office encryption formats, so its crypto helper silences
the .NET analyzer twice per algorithm: `CA5350` ("weak" — SHA1, 3DES) and `CA5351` ("broken" —
MD5, RC2, DES). Suppose we only want to review the suppressions of the *broken* ones.

`#pragma` lines are preprocessor directives: they never become part of the syntax tree, so no
`pattern:` can match them and `pattern-regex` is the only option. The starter finds all four
`#pragma warning disable` lines. The regex is compiled in multiline mode, which is why `^`
anchors it to the start of a *line*.

A regex can do more than match: a **named capturing group** `(?P<NAME>...)` binds the text it
captures to the metavariable `$NAME`, which you can then use in the message and in other
operators. Change `\w+` into a group that binds the warning code to `$CODE`, then add a
`metavariable-regex` on `$CODE` that keeps only `CA5351`.
hints: The group name becomes the metavariable: `(?P<CODE>\w+)` binds `$CODE`. Python-style `(?P<...>)` is the syntax Semgrep documents; plain `(?<CODE>...)` works too.
Then filter the binding like any other metavariable: `- metavariable-regex:` with `metavariable: $CODE` and `regex: CA5351`.
challenges.followup:
Two operators cooperated: `pattern-regex` matched the directive and, through the named group,
bound `$CODE` to `CA5350` or `CA5351`; `metavariable-regex` then kept the bindings that match
`CA5351` — and the message can say which code was suppressed. A metavariable bound by a regex is
plain text, not a syntax node, so it works with `metavariable-regex` but not with
`metavariable-pattern`, `metavariable-comparison` or `metavariable-analysis`, which need
something the parser produced.

The `restore` lines were never in danger: the regex spells out `disable`. And `^` did real work —
without it the directive text would also be found inside a string or a comment that quotes it.

**Try this:** change the filter to `regex: '5351'`: no matches, because `metavariable-regex` is
left-anchored and `$CODE` starts with `CA`; `.*5351` brings them back. Then capture only the
number, `CA(?P<NUM>\d+)`, and use `regex: '53(50|51)'` on `$NUM` to report both categories.

challenges.title: metavariable-regex with a lookahead — "anything but https"
challenges.instructions:
These ASP.NET Core tests register CORS origins through `new CorsPolicyBuilder(...)` and
`builder.WithOrigins(...)`. We want every origin *literal* that is not an `https://` URL —
`http://example.com`, `http://*.example.com` and friends — while `"HTTPS://example2.com"` is
fine: schemes are case-insensitive, and the builder normalises it.

Saying "not https" in a regex calls for a **negative lookahead**, `(?!...)`. The starter uses
one — and reports far too much: `new CorsPolicyBuilder(originalPolicy)` and
`builder.WithOrigins(args)` are flagged although they pass no literal at all. Remember two
things about `metavariable-regex`: it sees the *source text* of the binding, quotes included,
and it is left-anchored — the regex is tried only at the start of that text.

Change the regex so that only string literals whose scheme is not `https://` match, in any
letter case.
hints: A lookahead consumes nothing, so `(?!"https://)` succeeds at the start of *every* binding that does not begin with `"https://` — including plain identifiers. Require the opening quote first, then look ahead.
`regex: '(?i)"(?!https://)'` — the `"` restricts the match to literals, the lookahead excludes the secure ones, `(?i)` makes it case-insensitive.
challenges.followup:
Read the regex from the left: `(?i)` switches on case-insensitivity for everything that follows;
`"` must be the first character of the binding (left-anchoring does the rest — no `^` needed), so
`originalPolicy` and `args` are out; `(?!https://)` then peeks at the text after the quote
without consuming it and fails for `"HTTPS://example2.com"`. A lookahead is the idiomatic way
to say "does not start with" inside a single regex; the alternative is a positive pattern such as
`"http://` — shorter, but silent about `ftp://`, `ws://` or a scheme-less `"example.com"`.

Notice what the starter got wrong twice on the same line: `new CorsPolicyBuilder("http://www.EXAMPLE.com", "HTTPS://example2.com")`
was reported for *both* arguments, because the case-sensitive `(?!"https://)` let `"HTTPS://`
through. Grading is by line, so that bug only shows in the number of findings — add `$ORIGIN`
to the message and count them.

**Try this:** the `Assert.Equal(new List<string>() { "http://example.com", ... })` lines contain
the same literals and are never reported — the syntax patterns decide *where* to look, the regex
only decides *what* is acceptable. Replace the whole rule with `pattern-regex: '"http://'` and
watch the assertions and `IsOriginAllowed(...)` calls light up too.

challenges.instructions:
Json.NET's `TypeNameHandling` setting decides whether a JSON document may name the .NET type to
instantiate. Anything other than `None` has been the root of a long list of deserialization
advisories. These two helpers from Json.NET's own test suite set it once to `None` and once to
`All` inside object initializers.

The starter matches both assignments. We want to look *inside* what `$V` captured and keep only
values that are **not** `TypeNameHandling.None`. `metavariable-pattern` does exactly that: it runs
a nested pattern block — `pattern`, `patterns` or `pattern-either` (a `pattern-not` is only
allowed inside that nested `patterns:` list) — on the captured expression, as if it were a tiny
file of its own.

Add a `metavariable-pattern` entry on `$V` whose nested `patterns:` accepts `TypeNameHandling.$MODE`
but rejects `TypeNameHandling.None`.
hints: Under `patterns:` add `- metavariable-pattern:` with `metavariable: $V` and a nested `patterns:` list.
The nested list needs a positive pattern (`TypeNameHandling.$MODE`) and a `pattern-not: TypeNameHandling.None`.
challenges.followup:
The outer pattern `TypeNameHandling = $V` matches an assignment wherever it appears — here inside
an object initializer. The nested `patterns:` then operate on `$V` alone: `TypeNameHandling.$MODE`

`pattern-not: TypeNameHandling.None` removes the safe one. `All`, `Objects`, `Arrays` and `Auto`
all remain.

instead. `metavariable-pattern` pays off when the check is more complex than one negation, when the
same binding must satisfy several conditions, or — as in the next challenge — when the captured
text must be analysed in another language.

challenges.title: metavariable-pattern with another language
challenges.instructions:
`RunCompile` compiles a Razor template *at runtime*. The template is a C# string — but its
*content* is Razor, and we would like to look inside it for `@Model.<something>`.

`metavariable-pattern` runs a nested pattern on what a metavariable captured. With a `language:`
key the nested pattern is matched in a different language — here `generic`, Semgrep's token-based
mode for text without a parser. Because it works on the *captured text*, the rule first captures
the literal where it is written (`string $T = $LIT;` as a `pattern-inside`) and then inspects
`$LIT`; the call itself only refers to the variable `template`.

The starter looks for `@Html.Raw` inside the template and finds nothing. Change the nested
pattern so that a template reading any property of `@Model` is reported.
hints: Only the nested `pattern:` under `metavariable-pattern` needs to change.
Generic mode matches tokens: `@Model.$PROP` matches `@Model.Name`, `@Model.Email`, …
challenges.followup:
Three things cooperate here. `pattern-inside` binds `$T` to `template` and `$LIT` to the literal
`"Hello @Model.Name, welcome to RazorEngine!"`; the main pattern requires the call to use `$T`;
and `metavariable-pattern` with `language: generic` runs `@Model.$PROP` over the literal's text
as tokens, where `$PROP` matches `Name`.

Why not simply inspect `$T`? `metavariable-pattern` looks at the captured *source text* —
`template`, an identifier — not at the value constant propagation would assign to it. Capturing
the literal at its declaration is the reliable way to get the text.

`language:` accepts any Semgrep language, so a SQL string could be inspected with a `generic`
pattern like `SELECT ... FROM $TBL WHERE ... = ...`, and an inline JavaScript string with
`language: javascript` — real parsing, not a regex.

**Try this:** change the nested pattern to `welcome to $ENGINE!` — still a match, generic mode is
just tokens. Then drop `language: generic`: the nested pattern is now parsed as C#, where
`@Model.$PROP` is a member-access expression on the verbatim identifier `@Model`, and a
string literal contains no such expression — nothing matches.

challenges.title: metavariable-comparison — arithmetic on a captured number
challenges.instructions:
Two expiry times computed with `DateTime.Now.AddMinutes(...)`: a JWT that lives 30 minutes
(dvcsharp-api) and a cookie that lives 10 (IssueBlot). Suppose policy says nothing may live longer
than 15 minutes. The starter captures the number in `$N` but reports both.

`metavariable-comparison` evaluates a small expression over a captured value — numbers and
strings, plus a few helper functions — and keeps the match only if it is true. The expression uses
the metavariable by name: `$N > 15`, `$N * 60 > 900`, `$N != 0` and so on.

Add a `metavariable-comparison` entry so that only the 30-minute token is reported.
hints: Under `patterns:` add `- metavariable-comparison:` with two keys: `metavariable: $N` and `comparison: ...`.
`comparison: $N > 15`.
challenges.followup:
`$N` is bound to the literal `30` in one call and `10` in the other; the comparison `$N > 15`
holds only for the first. The comparison language is a Python-like expression evaluator: numeric
operators, `and` / `or` / `not`, and a few helpers such as `int(...)`, `str(...)`, `today()` and
`re.match(...)` — `re.match("^3", str($N))` would single out the same call. That Python-like
syntax is also why the browser engine here ships a small Python parser.

Comparisons need a value they can evaluate. A literal works, and so does a local that constant
propagation resolves to one (`int n = 30; ... AddMinutes(n)` is still reported). If the argument is
something Semgrep cannot resolve — a parameter, `AddMinutes(lifetime)` — the comparison fails and
the match is dropped; a comparison cannot help there, so match the call without it or track the
value with a taint rule.

**Try this:** use `comparison: $N > 15 and $N < 60` — same result. Then compare in seconds
instead, `comparison: $N * 60 > 900` — still only the 30-minute token (1800 > 900, but 600 is not).

challenges.title: metavariable-analysis — entropy instead of a regex
challenges.instructions:
Same four constants as in the `metavariable-regex` challenge, different tool. A regex for "32+ hex
digits" only finds secrets that happen to be hex. Real secrets come in many shapes; what they have in
common is that they look *random*.

`metavariable-analysis` runs a built-in analyzer over a captured value. The `entropy` analyzer
reports strings whose character distribution looks random enough to be a key or token; the `redos`
analyzer flags regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. Those are the two the
open-source engine implements — the rule schema also accepts `entropy_v2`, but that one needs the
Pro engine and quietly matches nothing in the plain CLI.

Add a `metavariable-analysis` entry under `patterns:` so that only the high-entropy `TokenSecret`
matches and the three role names do not.
hints: The entry takes two keys: `metavariable:` names the capture to inspect and `analyzer:` names the built-in check. You want the *value*, not the name, and the analyzer that measures randomness.
`- metavariable-analysis: {metavariable: $V, analyzer: entropy}`
challenges.followup:
Entropy analysis has no idea what a secret *is* — it just measures how unpredictable the characters
are. `"User"` and `"Administrator"` are ordinary English; `"f449a71c…"` is not. This is how
Semgrep's generic-secrets rules and many secret scanners work, and it complements name-based and
format-based checks rather than replacing them.

**Try this:** add a fifth constant `public const string Greeting = "hello hello hello";` to the
target in your local checkout — low entropy, no match. Then paste a real API key or a long
base64 blob — the analyzer flags it, no hex required. It is only a heuristic, though:
`"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"` is flagged as well — letter-diverse English looks
random enough — while `"http://localhost.local/"` is not.

challenges.title: fix — a rule that repairs what it finds
challenges.instructions:
The JWT issued by this method expires at `DateTime.Now.AddMinutes(30)`. `DateTime.Now` is the
server's *local* time, while JWT lifetimes (`exp`, `nbf`) are expressed in UTC. Mixing the two is a
classic source of off-by-a-time-zone bugs — DST transitions, or a later comparison against
`DateTime.UtcNow` somewhere else — so the safe spelling is `DateTime.UtcNow`.

The starter rule already finds the line; this challenge is graded on the **fix**. Change the rule
by adding a `fix:` key so that `semgrep --autofix` would rewrite the match to `DateTime.UtcNow`.

A `fix:` is plain replacement text for the matched range. It may mention metavariables from the
pattern (`$X`), which are substituted with what they captured.
hints: The replacement text goes in a key of its own, at the same level as `pattern:` and `message:`. Only the matched range (`DateTime.Now`) is replaced, so do not repeat `.AddMinutes(30)`.
Add a rule-level key next to `pattern:`: `fix: DateTime.UtcNow`.
challenges.followup:
Semgrep replaces exactly the matched range — `DateTime.Now`, not the whole line — with the fix text,
so `.AddMinutes(30)` survives. On the command line, `semgrep --config rule.yaml --autofix` applies
it; without `--autofix` the suggested fix is shown alongside the finding. In the browser results
panel you can see the rendered fix under each match.

Fixes really shine with metavariables: a pattern `DateTime.Now.AddMinutes($N)` with
`fix: DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes($N)` keeps whatever number was there.

**Try this:** change the pattern to `$D.Now` with `fix: $D.UtcNow` — same match, and the fix is
now generic over the receiver.

challenges.title: fix-regex — and fixes with metavariables
challenges.instructions:
Umbraco normalises e-mail addresses with `email.ToLower().Trim()`. `ToLower()` uses the
*current culture*: on a Turkish system `"I".ToLower()` is `"ı"` (dotless i), so two spellings of
the same address may stop comparing equal. For identifiers the right call is
`ToLowerInvariant()`.

The starter has a `fix:` that changes nothing (it re-emits the match). There are two ways to write
the real fix:

* `fix: $S.ToLowerInvariant()` — rebuild the replacement from the pattern's metavariables.
* `fix-regex:` — apply a regular-expression substitution to the matched text, with `regex:` and
  `replacement:` keys. Handy when the match is long and only a small part changes.

Change the starter's `fix:` into a `fix-regex:` that rewrites `ToLower()` to `ToLowerInvariant()`.
The challenge is graded on the rendered fix text.
hints: `fix-regex:` is a mapping with two keys: `regex:` and `replacement:`.
`regex: 'ToLower\(\)'` — escape the parentheses; `replacement: 'ToLowerInvariant()'`.
challenges.followup:
Both matches are rewritten to `email.ToLowerInvariant()`: the regex runs on the matched range only
(`email.ToLower()`), never on the whole file, so the `.Trim()` after it is untouched. `fix-regex`
also accepts `count:` to limit the number of substitutions, and the replacement may use `\1`-style
backreferences.

`fix: $S.ToLowerInvariant()` would produce the identical result here and is usually easier to read;
reach for `fix-regex` when the change is a small edit inside a large match, or when the
replacement depends on text that no metavariable captures.

**Try this:** switch to `fix: $S.ToLowerInvariant()` — same rendered fixes, still correct. Then
change the pattern to `$S.ToLower().Trim()` with `fix: $S.ToLowerInvariant().Trim()`: the match
grows to include `.Trim()` and the fix has to reproduce it. The checker now reports the rendered
fix `email.ToLowerInvariant().Trim()` as different from the reference `email.ToLowerInvariant()` —
expected, since fixes are graded as text.

challenges.title: Taint mode — sources and sinks
challenges.instructions:
Two SQLite queries in this deliberately vulnerable controller. The one in `SQLInjection`
interpolates two request parameters into the SQL; the one in `SecurityMisconfiguration` is a
constant. A *search* rule for `new SQLiteCommand($Q, ...)` — the starter — cannot tell them
apart, because it only looks at the shape of the call.

**Taint mode** looks at *data flow* instead. A rule with `mode: taint` lists `pattern-sources`
(where untrusted data enters — here `RequestUtils.GetIfDefined(Request, "...")`) and
`pattern-sinks` (where it must not arrive). Semgrep then reports a sink only if some source
flows into it, through assignments, string interpolation, concatenation and method arguments.

Rewrite the starter as a taint rule: the request helper is the source, and the query argument of
`new SQLiteCommand(...)` is the sink. Use `focus-metavariable` in the sink so that only the SQL
argument counts.
hints: Add `mode: taint`, then replace `pattern:` with `pattern-sources:` and `pattern-sinks:` lists.
Source: `- pattern: RequestUtils.GetIfDefined(Request, "...")`.
Sink: `- patterns:` with `- pattern: new SQLiteCommand($Q, ...)` and `- focus-metavariable: $Q`.
challenges.followup:
`name` and `pw` are tainted at the source; the interpolated string that embeds them is tainted
too, and it is passed as `$Q` — a sink. The constant query never touches a source, so it is not
reported even though it is the same API. That is the whole idea of taint analysis: same sink,
different verdict, depending on where the data came from.

Each entry under `pattern-sources` / `pattern-sinks` is a full pattern block, so `patterns:` with
`focus-metavariable` is how you say "the *argument* is the sink, not the whole call". Semgrep's
taint tracking is intraprocedural in the OSS engine: it follows data within one method only. A
call with a tainted argument, such as `Helper(name)`, is simply *assumed* to return tainted data —
the helper's body is never analysed, so a source hidden inside a helper is missed, and a helper
that discards its input still counts as a flow. Cross-function tracking is a Pro-engine feature.

**Try this:** add `- pattern: $DB.ExecuteReader()` as a second sink — a second finding appears on
`using (var reader = command.ExecuteReader())` in `SQLInjection`, because `command` was built from
tainted data, while the `ExecuteReader()` in `SecurityMisconfiguration` stays clean for the same
reason. Then remove `focus-metavariable`: the first finding grows to cover the whole
`new SQLiteCommand(...)`.

challenges.title: Taint mode — sanitizers and propagators
challenges.instructions:
Two flows in this controller, and the starter gets both wrong.

In `SQLInjection`, request data flows through the query into `reader`, into `res`, and into
`Show(...)` — but it passes through `_javaScriptEncoder.Encode(...)` first. The starter reports
that call anyway. A **sanitizer** is a pattern whose result is considered clean; add
`pattern-sanitizers` so that encoded values no longer count.

In `XXE`, the request XML goes into `xmlDoc.LoadXml(xml)`. Nothing is *returned* from that call,
so as far as default taint tracking is concerned `xmlDoc` stays clean and iterating it with
`foreach` — the second sink — is never reported. A **propagator** teaches Semgrep that a call
moves taint from one argument to another object: `pattern-propagators` with `from:` and `to:`.
Add one for `LoadXml`.

Expected result: exactly one finding, the `foreach` over the document; every `Show(...)` is clean.
hints: Both new keys sit at the same level as `pattern-sources:` / `pattern-sinks:`. A sanitizer names an expression whose *result* is clean; a propagator names a call that *carries* taint from one argument to another.
`pattern-sanitizers:` takes the same kind of entries as sinks: `- pattern: _javaScriptEncoder.Encode(...)`.
`pattern-propagators:` entries need three keys: `pattern: $DOC.LoadXml($XML)`, `from: $XML`, `to: $DOC`.
challenges.followup:
Sanitizers cut a flow: whatever `_javaScriptEncoder.Encode(...)` returns is clean, so the
`Show(...)` call that only receives encoded data stops being reported. Propagators extend a flow:
`xmlDoc.LoadXml(xml)` returns nothing, so without the propagator the document would never be
tainted; with `from: $XML` / `to: $DOC` the taint of the argument is copied onto the receiver by
side effect, and the `foreach` over `xmlDoc` is now a tainted sink.

Note the line inside the loop: `xn` is tainted too (Semgrep follows `foreach`), but the
`Show(...)` there only receives `_javaScriptEncoder.Encode(xn.InnerText)`, which the sanitizer
cleans — so it stays quiet.

Propagators are how registry rules model `StringBuilder.Append`, `List.Add`, `Dictionary` writes
and similar "taint goes in here, comes out there" APIs.

**Try this:** delete the sanitizer and keep the propagator — three findings, since both encoded
`Show(...)` calls are reported again. Then change the propagator's `to:` to `$XML`: only the
`Show(...)` in `SQLInjection` is left — `$XML` was tainted already, so nothing new is propagated
and the document stays clean.

challenges.title: Taint mode — by-side-effect, unification and the rest of the rule file
challenges.instructions:
SSH.NET's SCP download loop reads chunks from the channel stream into `buffer` and writes them
straight to the output stream. (This excerpt is from the commit just before the fix for
[GHSA-q939-rpr3-3284](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q939-rpr3-3284); the rule illustrates the
general "read from the network, pass on unchecked" shape rather than that specific bug.)

The starter is a complete, production-style rule: `metadata` with a CWE and a reference,
`min-version`, `severity`, and a taint rule whose source focuses on the buffer argument of
`Read` and whose sink focuses on the buffer argument of `Write` — the *same* buffer, enforced by
`options.taint_unify_mvars`. It finds nothing.

The reason: `input.Read(buffer, ...)` does not *return* the data, it fills `buffer` **by side
effect**. Semgrep only considers a source's *result* tainted unless you say otherwise. Add
`by-side-effect: true` to the source so that the focused `$BUF` is tainted after the call.
hints: The key goes on the source entry, next to `patterns:` (same indentation): `by-side-effect: true`.
Nothing else changes — unification already makes sure `$BUF` is the same variable at the sink.
challenges.followup:
With `by-side-effect: true`, the source entry says: after `input.Read(buffer, …)` runs, the
variable bound to `$BUF` is tainted, even though the call returned an `int`. From there the flow to
`output.Write(buffer, 0, read)` is direct.

`options.taint_unify_mvars: true` requires metavariables that appear in both the source and the
sink to bind to the same thing — here `$BUF` — so a write of some *other* buffer would not be
reported. Without it, source and sink metavariables are independent.

The other keys are documentation and control, not matching: `metadata` travels with every finding
(CWE, references, categories), `min-version` makes older CLIs skip a rule that uses newer syntax,
and `severity` sets the finding level. Sinks also accept `exact`, and its default for sinks is
`true` (the opposite of sources and sanitizers): for a call sink such as `$OUT.Write($BUF, ...)`
the call's *arguments* are the sinks, which is why the unfocused form fires when only `buffer` is
tainted; taint that sits inside an argument without flowing into its value (the docs' example is
`sink("foo" if tainted else "bar")`) only counts with `exact: false`.

**Try this:** remove `options:` — still one finding here, because there is only one buffer. Then
drop `focus-metavariable` from the sink and remove `by-side-effect` again: the finding comes back,
because now the *whole* `output.Write(buffer, 0, read)` call is the sink, every argument counts, and
`read` is tainted — it is the result of `input.Read(buffer, ...)`, a call whose argument is the
source. Focusing the sink is what made the side effect matter.
